note: Stage 1 candidates and tests. On master: the heterosynaptic write (SPEC 8.16, passed its kill test on three seeds) with its off-by-default parent encode-mode (8.12) and the 8.15 diagnostics; both flags are off by default and the default plant is unchanged Stage 0. Rejected candidates stay on unmerged branches. K1.1 pattern completion still fails. The combined-mechanisms experiment (SPEC 8.17, inhibition as the hippocampal rate controller) was rejected on three seeds and is not merged. A diagnostic (SPEC 8.18) then traced the 8.17 readout loss to the cortex: the homeostat suppresses the answer to a stimulus within seconds of showing it. An ablation (SPEC 8.19) showed that slowing the homeostat removes most of that suppression and keeps the plant in band, but trained cells still do not answer more than untrained ones: on this plant the pair rule weakens synapses between co-active cells. An offline evaluation (SPEC 8.20) measured that directly and found that the published triplet rule (hippocampal set) would strengthen the driven pathway instead. Built and tested (SPEC 8.21), that rule was rejected on three seeds: trained cells did out-fire untrained ones for the first time and the plant stayed stable, but the gain was small and unspecific and weights piled up at their bound; not merged. A follow-up diagnostic (SPEC 8.22) confirmed that small gain with learning frozen during the readout, and screened two more published rules offline: neither qualified. The cause found: a stimulus raises almost the whole cortex, so no rule that works at a single synapse can tell the stimulus's inputs from the rest by more than about a factor of two. A ceiling test (SPEC 8.23) then set the existing connections to their maximum by hand: even so a half cue recalls only 8 to 11 of the 16 memory cells in the allowed time, and the same strong connections make them fire with no cue. On the present wiring the recall test cannot be passed by learning alone; the wiring or size has to change. What-if brains (SPEC 8.24): giving the memory region four times as many internal connections keeps it healthy and lets a half cue recall the memory within 200 ms at the ceiling, but not within the 50 ms the test allows; simply asking the cortex to be quieter made the brain unhealthy. A second-generation brain was then built on a branch only (SPEC 8.25): quieter cortex, denser memory-region wiring. Its activity is healthy on three seeds, but one Stage 0 test (a storage-capacity check with a fixed size) fails on it, so by the rule set in advance the branch is marked failed. At the hand-set ceiling a half cue recalls the memory within 200 ms on every seed, and within the official 50 ms on one seed of three; the official recall test K1.1 remains failed. The storage-capacity check was then rewritten on that branch to size itself from the brain's own wiring, and the second-generation brain passes the same health checks as today's (SPEC 8.26). Learned recall was then measured on it with the existing learning rules, beside a twin that was never trained: no rule gives recall from a half cue; the plain rule makes it worse than no training, and the triplet rule makes the brain run away on one seed. K1.1 remains failed. A follow-up diagnostic (SPEC 8.27) found why training hurts on the second-generation brain: the two seconds of training weaken the very connections from cortex onto the memory cells that the cue needs (from about 92 % to 70 % of their maximum). Swapping just those connections between the trained brain and its untrained twin moves the whole deficit. This explains a failure; it is not recall, and K1.1 remains failed. The next experiment (SPEC 8.28) tried a stand-in rule built from that finding: cells that fire strongly keep their input strengths from the pair rule. On three seeds the trained brain then answers a half cue with 7 to 8 more of its 16 memory cells than an untrained twin within 50 ms, without answering the wrong pattern or firing when idle; about half the gain is left after a sleep. This is a test-side stand-in, not yet a mechanism in the engine, and the official recall test K1.1 was not run and remains failed.
